chapter.title: The CEO Room
chapter.sub: Thirty seconds to save the room. A week to make sure it never happens in any room.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the season map (MS-02) ahead of its production-bible entry · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 3 · EPISODE 10 · DRAFT · SEASON FINALE  Countdown · MS-02 · Maya, Imani and Sam · Level L3 (Technician)  Monday, 9:00. The CEO opens the board meeting. Investors are dialed in. She shares her chart — and they see nothing. Thirty seconds to save the room. A week to make sure it never happens in any room.  ⚑ RV-77 · RV-78: the capture behavior, update and every number are illustrative. Changes to a live room wait for the change process. Most choices in this episode run on a clock — one of them on fifteen seconds.

items.title: Thirty Seconds
items.stakes: Twelve board members in the room. Eight investors on the line. The investors see a blank window. Thirty seconds of dead air and Dana will notice. So will the markets.
items.reward: Saved, then solved. A label that outlived an argument.

objectives.text: Read three readings in six seconds
Find why the test ring passed
Plan the fleet before the change board
Choose the five rooms that look like four hundred
Look closer: three things the week uncovers

items.rumor: On the ingest box under the table is a five-year-old label. Maya would know that font anywhere.

items.alt: The boardroom. Dana Whitcomb, the CEO, stands at the head of the long table, pointing to her chart on the big display: Q3, ahead of plan. Ines, her executive assistant, stands by the wall with a tablet. A countdown reads 00:30.

bubbles.text: Let me share the quarter with everyone — including our friends on the line.
(…Maya.)

items.caption: Twelve board members in the room. Eight investors on the line (illustrative). One chart.

items.alt: Close on Ines's tablet, which shows what the far end sees: four investor tiles and a large content window that is completely black. Ines, beside it, whispers.

bubbles.text: Maya. The investors see a blank window. Thirty seconds of dead air and she'll notice.

items.caption: The room sees the chart. The people the chart is for see nothing.

items.alt: The back of the boardroom. Maya, listening hard; the table's touch panel reads SHARING. Sam, crouched by the table end, holds up the HDMI cable he's just swapped.

bubbles.text: Local shows it. Panel says Sharing. Far end: nothing.
Swapped the table cable already. No change.

items.caption: Three readings. The room is telling them exactly where the break is — if they can hear it.

lines.text: Swapped the table cable already. No change.
Local shows it. Panel says Sharing. Far end: nothing.
(Her hands are shaking. Her voice isn't. She has no idea how.)

items.prompt: 00:26. Local display: chart. Panel: Sharing. Far end: blank. Cable swapped, no change. What does that tell you?
items.happening: The local display shows the chart; the far end sees a blank content window.
unknown: What the room computer is capturing
items.risk: A CEO, a board and eight investors.
timeout: Sam, out of ideas, reaches for the room's power button. Maya grabs his wrist just in time — five more seconds gone.
When nobody reads the evidence out loud, somebody reaches for the reboot.

hints.text: Two different things are fed: the display, and the far end. Which one is wrong?

options.label: The cable's still bad — swap it again
options.result: Sam swaps it again. The local display blinks; Dana glances at it. Far end: still blank.
options.consequence: The local display already proved the cable. Now the CEO has noticed something.
options.fail: The local path works. The cable can't be the break.

options.label: The investors' internet is slow — the guest Wi-Fi speed test is awful
options.result: The speed test is awful. The room's call isn't on guest Wi-Fi.
options.consequence: A red herring that feels like evidence.
options.fail: Measuring the wrong path proves nothing about this one.

options.label: The room computer is sending the far end something other than what the display shows — look at what it's capturing
options.result: Two paths: table → switcher → display (fine), and capture → room computer → far end (wrong). Look under the table.
options.consequence: The break is split in half in one sentence.

options.label: The calendar warned about something this morning — check that
options.fail: Reading banners while the clock runs.

items.alt: Under the table, in Sam's flashlight beam: a gray ingest box with two inputs, IN 1 and IN 2. Below them, two label-maker labels: IN 1 = TABLE HDMI. IN 2 = TABLE CUBBY.

bubbles.text: Two inputs. There's a label. “IN 2 = TABLE CUBBY.”

items.caption: Label-maker tape, five years old. Maya would know that font anywhere.

items.alt: Extreme close-up: the label, IN 2 = TABLE CUBBY, and in faded pen beside it, the initial R.
narration: Ray's label. Ray's label maker. The one he gave her.
items.caption: “Label everything,” he'd written. “Especially what only I know.”

items.title: “IN 2 = TABLE CUBBY”
items.body: Label-maker tape, five years old, in Ray's font. On the back, only visible when Sam peels it to read it: *— in case I'm not here. R.* He wrote it for exactly this Monday.

items.prompt: 00:15. FIFTEEN SECONDS. Dana is mid-sentence. The investors see nothing. Do it.
items.happening: A labeled second input, a documented laptop fallback, a reboot, a rollback.
known: ◉ Laptop join is the documented fallback
items.risk: The CEO's credibility with her investors, live.
timeout: The fifteen seconds run out. Dana pauses: “Is everyone seeing this?” A voice on the line: “…No?”
She noticed. The only choice that loses for certain is none.

options.label: Reboot the room
options.result: The call drops. The display goes black in front of the board. Three minutes, minimum, of dead air — and the room rejoins with the same update.
options.consequence: Dana stops mid-word. The investors wait, then start texting.
options.fail: Three minutes you didn't have, and it doesn't touch the cause.

options.label: Ines: Dana's laptop joins the call directly and shares
options.result: A soft join tone. Ines taps Share on the laptop. The chart appears for the far end in about twenty seconds.
options.consequence: The documented fallback. It works — just a little slower and a little louder.

options.label: Sam moves Dana's cable to the table cubby — IN 2
options.result: Two seconds of hands under the table. Dana never looks down. On Ines's tablet, the chart appears.
options.consequence: The labeled path, found through the label. Nothing restarted, nothing noticed.

options.label: Roll back last night's update from the admin console
options.result: The rollback starts on a live room. The call stutters. Nobody approved this.
options.consequence: An unauthorized change to the CEO's room, mid-meeting, with investors watching.
options.fail: Change policy is binding — especially here, especially now.

items.alt: Under the table, Sam slides the CEO's cable into IN 2. The IN 2 port lights green.
items.caption: Two seconds of hands under a table. Nobody above it knew.

items.alt: Ines's tablet: the far-end content window now shows the chart. Ines, still whispering, smiles.

bubbles.text: They see it.

evidence.label: investor, side channel: “Q3, ahead of plan”

items.alt: Dana, at the head of the table, sweeps a hand toward the chart, confident.

bubbles.text: …and as you can see, the quarter closed ahead of plan.

items.caption: Twenty-seven seconds. She never knew.

items.alt: In the corridor outside the boardroom, Maya stands alone, hands at her sides, not quite steady.
narration: Maya's hands didn't stop shaking until 9:20.
items.caption: Saved. Not solved.

lines.text: (Her hands don't stop shaking until 9:20. Nobody in the room knows. That's the job. It's also the loneliest part of it.)

items.label: **Service Mode:** 9:00:40. Run the thirty seconds yourself. (Relaxed timers double the clock.)

items.sub: 9:40 · the corridor, then the service desk

items.alt: Imani finds Maya in the corridor.

bubbles.text: Thirty seconds. Brilliant. Now make sure it never happens again — in any room.
Which rooms?

items.caption: “That's the question,” Imani says. “You have a week.”

items.prompt: Thirty seconds. Brilliant. Now make sure it never happens again — in any room. Where do you start?

options.label: “With the rooms nobody's watching. The eleven.”
options.reply: Good. That's the answer I'd have written on the whiteboard.

options.label: “With the update. Roll it back everywhere.”
options.reply: Everywhere includes three hundred rooms that are fine.

options.label: “Can I have a minute? I'm still shaking.”
options.reply: Take five. Then the eleven. I'll get coffee.

items.title: Building the fallback from what's on board
items.body: In April 1970, after an oxygen tank exploded on Apollo 13, the three astronauts sheltered in the lunar module, whose carbon-dioxide scrubbers weren't meant for three people for four days. The command module had spare scrubber cartridges — square, where the lunar module's sockets were round. Engineers on the ground built an adapter from things they knew were aboard: plastic bags, cardboard, hoses and tape, then read the steps up to the crew. A fallback is only as good as what's really in the room — and whether someone wrote down how to use it.

items.alt: The boardroom computer's records on a service-desk monitor, read-only: an update package installed at 02:10, ring: fleet. Capture inputs IN 1 and IN 2; content now IN 2, 'first detected'. Update notes: the default content input is now the first input detected.
items.caption: Update history → two inputs → Ray's label → the notes. The evidence tree, in order.

items.alt: System View of the boardroom's content path after the update. The CEO's laptop feeds IN 1, the table HDMI. IN 1 feeds the switcher and the room display, which shows the chart. The room computer, after the 02:10 update, takes content from IN 2, the empty table cubby, and sends that to the far end, which is blank.
items.caption: Two paths from one table. The update moved one of them to an empty chair.

items.alt: The update's ring-1 test on a monitor: five standard rooms, Aspen through Fir, all passed; inputs per room, one. Nora points at the list.

bubbles.text: Five rooms, all pass. All five have one input. The boardroom wasn't in the ring — it isn't in the inventory. Exception room four.

items.caption: Every test passed. None of them could have failed.

items.title: The test ring passed
items.body: The update wasn't untested. It passed ring 1 cleanly — five standard rooms, each with a single content input, where “the first input detected” is always the right one. The failure needed a room with two inputs. The only rooms with two were the exceptions nobody had recorded, so none of them were in the ring. The boardroom was number four on Nora's list.
items.label: Test: reason from the ring. Why did it pass — and which rooms do you query now?

items.prompt: 9:52. Imani needs a plan for the fleet before the 10:30 change board. What do you propose?
items.happening: The boardroom is saved; the cause is in the fleet.
known: ◉ Boardroom not in ring or inventory
unknown: Which other rooms have two inputs
items.risk: Every room with the boardroom's shape.
timeout: The change board meets without a proposal and defaults to “monitor the situation.”
A week starts with one decision. Not making it spends a day.

hints.text: Fix the instance safely today; hunt the class this week.

options.label: Roll the update back on every room tonight
options.result: Three hundred rooms change overnight on a plan nobody has tested — and lose the security fixes the update carried.
options.fail: A fleet-wide rollback is a fleet-wide change. It needs its own test — and it undoes patches.

options.label: Emergency change today: pin the boardroom's content input explicitly; then query the fleet for every room with more than one input
options.result: The change board approves in twenty minutes. The boardroom's content input is set to IN 1 by name, not by default.
options.consequence: The CEO room is safe by lunch. The rest of the week goes to finding its twins.

options.label: Nothing — the cubby trick worked
options.result: Next Monday, Dana plugs into the table HDMI again.
options.consequence: The failure class is still in the building.
options.fail: You saved a meeting and left the cause in place.

options.label: Block all updates to the boardroom, permanently
options.result: Mei: “Then it's the one room in the building that never gets security patches.”
options.consequence: Exceptions made permanent become the next blind spot.
options.fail: Freezing a room trades one risk for a worse one.

items.label: **First failure point:** where does the content stop?

items.alt: Tuesday. A new exception register on a monitor: room, what differs, owner, in the ring? The boardroom has two inputs; Harbor a divisible wall; Studio its own computer build; eight more. Every owner column reads question marks; every ring column, no.

bubbles.text: Eleven rows. Every owner is a question mark.
Then that's Thursday's job.

items.sub: Beginner · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Ines and Maya beside a board. Update rings: a few rooms first, then more, so a bad update hurts a few people instead of everyone. The exception register lists every room that's different. How big is the next ring? What's left times the share. Two hundred rooms left, twenty-five percent: fifty rooms.

bubbles.text: Update rings: a few rooms first, then more, so a bad update hurts a few people instead of everyone. The exception register lists every room that's different.
How big is the next ring?
What's left times the share. Two hundred rooms left, twenty-five percent: fifty rooms.

items.caption: Beginner: the term, what it means, the formula — and one worked example out loud.

items.text: 📘 RAY'S NOTEBOOK · BEGINNER  Terms    Update ring   A group of systems updated together, smallest and least critical first.   Exception register   A list of every room or system that doesn't follow the standard, each with an owner and a reason.   Formula, variables and a worked example   ƒ FORMULA · Update ring size  ring = remaining rooms × share   remaining rooms  fleet minus rooms already in earlier rings  share  fraction for this ring (10% = 0.10)    Worked example.  200 rooms left, 25% ring: 200 × 0.25 = 50 rooms in this ring.

📒 EMPATHIA LEARN FIELDBOOK · MODULE 31 OF 31 · PP. 132–135, 160–163, 182  PART 8 VIDEO ENGINEERING · PART 10 LIGHTING ENGINEERING · PART 11 OPERATIONS  Page 182, the last page:  Good technology should disappear.  There were two names on the spine now, Ray's crossed out and Maya's under it — and room for a third.

items.label: **Learn it now:** update rings and exception registers.

items.alt: System View of the new update-ring design: ring 0, the lab, two rooms; ring 1, one room of every shape, five rooms; ring 2, a slice of forty rooms; ring 3, all four hundred. Ring 1 includes a standard room, a two-input room, a divisible room, a huddle room and a boardroom-type room, each with a far-end content check, a 24-hour watch, and a pause and rollback at every step.
items.caption: Wednesday. Five rooms that look like four hundred, instead of five that look like each other.

items.prompt: Wednesday. Which five rooms go in ring 1?

options.label: Five rooms picked at random from the fleet
options.result: Odds are all five are standard rooms. The ring passes every update again.
options.consequence: Random isn't representative when the rare rooms are the risky ones.
options.fail: You rebuilt the ring that missed the boardroom.

options.label: One room of every configuration: standard, two-input, divisible, huddle, boardroom-type
options.result: Every update now meets every shape of room before it meets the fleet.
options.consequence: A failure that needs two inputs has somewhere to fail.

options.label: Just the boardroom — it's the one that matters
options.result: The boardroom is safe. Harbor's divisible wall isn't.
options.consequence: You protected the CEO and nobody else.

options.label: All 400 rooms at once, with a rollback ready
options.result: That isn't a ring. It's the fleet.
options.consequence: Every surprise happens everywhere at once.
options.fail: A ring exists so a failure happens small first.

items.alt: Thursday. The empty boardroom. Ray, holding his small notebook, stands at one end of the table; Mei at the other.

bubbles.text: Imani said you need owners for the exception rooms. Most of them are mine. I built them.
Then let's put them in the register. Not in the notebook.

items.caption: The first time they'd been in a room since Saturday.

items.alt: Ray's notebook, open: Boardroom (D.W.) — IN 2 = table cubby, her side table; admin password, dotted out; Harbor: wall makes two rooms; Studio: own computer build; and in green, 'label it! — R'.
items.caption: Eleven exception rooms, each one a page in one man's notebook.

items.teaser: Ray's notebook, open on the table
items.title: Eleven pages, eleven rooms
items.body: Every exception room in the building, in one man's handwriting, with the reasons nobody else ever heard. The last page in the notebook isn't about Aldermoor at all: *Kestrel Valley — 2004 — backup MCR, REF B = house black. Keep it. Cal knows.*

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #31 · AVERY'S LENS  Put the fallback where eyes land  In a crisis, the recovery step must be visible exactly where people look.  Ray's label on the ingest box — IN 2 = TABLE CUBBY — was a thirty-second fallback printed where Sam's eyes landed.

items.alt: Ray turns to Maya, who has just come in. He speaks quietly.

bubbles.text: I made that label because I knew I'd forget. Never thought anyone else would need it. Your policy person saved my label.
You taught me to read labels. Before you taught me anything else.

items.caption: That was the whole apology. It was enough.

lines.text: Your policy person saved my label.
You taught me to read labels before you taught me anything else.

items.alt: Mei and Ray at the table, the register open on a laptop between them. Ray tears one page out of his notebook and hands it to her.

bubbles.text: Boardroom password: rotated, in the approved store, named accounts only. And your label goes in the register, word for word.
One page. The rest of this notebook is other people's buildings.

items.caption: One page came out of the notebook. The notebook went back in his pocket. (DEBT-002)

items.alt: A fleet query result late on Thursday: four rooms with more than one content input. The boardroom, pinned to IN 1. Harbor B and Studio, on the default. And Juniper — the pilot room for the new standard, version 1.0 — on the default.

bubbles.text: Juniper. That's the standard. Section 3.4 — two inputs, for reach.

items.title: The standard had the same shape
items.body: The fleet query didn't just find two more exception rooms. It found Juniper — the pilot of Maya's own room standard. Section 3.4 gives every new room two content inputs, table and wall, because Participant 2 couldn't reach the old one. With the same update and an unpinned default, version 1.0 would have shipped the boardroom's failure to four hundred rooms. The requirement was right. The default was the trap.
items.label: Test: reason from the query. What would have happened, what goes in the standard — and is the second input the mistake?

items.alt: The standard's revised page, version 1.1, section 3: two content inputs, table and wall, for reach; 3.4.1, content capture input set explicitly per room, never default; 3.4.2, checked in ring 1 after every update.
items.caption: The second input stays. Participant 2's line survives the week.

items.alt: A laminated card on the office wall: If the far end can't see your screen — 30 seconds. Keep talking; check the far-end view; try the other labeled input; or join from your laptop; confirm with one person. Sam holds a stack of copies; Imani nods.

bubbles.text: Four hundred of these. One under every table, next to the labels.
Laminated. Somebody will spill coffee on the first one by Tuesday.

items.caption: END OF SEASON 3 · The boss level first. Then a broadcast control room — and page 5.3.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  When the room says it's sharing, check what the far end sees. Split the path: local display versus what the room computer captures. In the meeting, restart nothing: use the labeled input or the documented laptop fallback, and confirm with one remote person on their own screen — never roll back an update mid-meeting. Then eliminate the failure class: record every exception, build rings that contain one room of every shape, pin the settings that matter instead of trusting defaults, query the fleet for the same shape, and leave a 30-second card under every table.

REFLECTION (optional)  · A label saved the CEO's meeting — written five years ago by someone who expected to forget, and read by someone he once taught. What will someone else need from you in five years that only you know today?  Boundary: this reflection doesn't prove anything about the rooms.
